event: VXE-880 (35X fuselage with fuel cell 4500856) had the fuel cell stop for lack of fuel after 6 h 32 min of an endurance flight while the GCS still showed about 100 g remaining, and the operator landed.
component: fuel remaining estimate (flow meter based, no tank level sensor)
failure_mode: fuel exhaustion (starvation) while the estimated fuel remaining was still above zero, within the measurement error of the system
contributing: no direct fuel level measurement on VXE
flow meter accuracy about 5% (about 45 g on 900 g)
possible weighing errors of tank and fuel
fuel cell not supported or flight qualified on B35X configuration
flight planned for 8+ hours

evidence.quote: Data indicates fuel starvation. Fuel PWM, fuelset & fuelreal all indicate no fuel available to fuel cell.
It appears we just ran out of fuel during flight with the system indicating it still had ~100g remaining.
As of today, VXE systems do not have a method to measure actual fuel remaining (no special tank float sensors).
I see starting fuel was set to 926, the system landed with >0g (~100g).
Fuel Cell is not supported in B35x configuration - it has never been tested or flight qualified.

team_root_cause: Fuel starvation resulting in operator performing landing. Fuel remaining measurement likely within overall system error margin which resulted in system indicating fuel remaining when no actual fuel was remaining in tank.

would_settle_it.what: fuelset versus fuelreal and fuel PWM at the end of the flight
rule out a leak in the fuel cell plumbing, which the team chose not to do

reasoning: Fuel cell logs show fuel PWM railing high and fuelreal dropping below fuelset, meaning the cell asked for fuel and got none. The landed estimate of about 100 g is inside the stated flow meter error, and the system has no direct level sensor, so the tank most likely ran dry while the estimate still showed fuel. A leak was not checked, which is the one remaining alternative.
notes: Description says remaining fuel went from 200 g to zero; the engineer says the data does not match and shows about 100 g at landing. Aircraft was a 35X fuselage with standard 30 center wing, a configuration not qualified for fuel cell.

event: Master ticket for repeated hybrid lift battery cell voltage dropouts in flight across many aircraft (VXE-758, 880, 808, 674, 757, 689, 559 and others), causing aborted launches and hard landings.
failure_mode: dry cells from inadequate electrolyte (poor pouch hermetic seal, electrolyte evaporation), giving high cell impedance and voltage dropout under high VTOL load
contributing: not detectable in outgoing testing
degrades over battery life and storage
all affected batteries had 2024 manufacture dates
SEI formation and break-in still under investigation

evidence.quote: suggests the root cause of the poor electrical performance is inadequate electrolyte volume, causing high ohmic and concentration polarization.
It is currently suspected that the observed cell dryness is from a pouch sealing issue during cell manufacturing.
Pouch looseness was observed, suggesting the cells are not adequately hermetically sealed
Primary issue seems to be poorly sealed cells. Same cell series as B30, different capacity.
Voltage Drop Out is Primarily a Concentration caused Phenomenon (Electrolyte Loss)
Stephen has identified that the primary loss of function in the battery results in a higher cell or pack impedance

team_root_cause:
Battery Dissection led to discovery of leaking / evaporating electrolyte material inside the 3300mAh Advanced Energy Cells within the HLB. Including one instance of the Z-fold being caught in the pouch’s hermetic seal resulting in air passing through and reduced performance.
This evaporation can occur over time and would likely not be detectable in outgoing testing and would propagate over the course of the life of the battery. This is one of multiple possible contributing factors that affect battery performance, and additional analysis will circulate around the emphasis on quality control and

would_settle_it.what: full 8D findings and vendor (Tree Town Tech, Advanced Energy) cell RCA results
DCIR and self discharge results across the affected battery serials

reasoning: Teardown of failed cells (2-3785-2A, 2-4415-6B) found loose pouches, unsaturated separators and electrolyte decomposition deposits, while a good cell had normal electrolyte. The test plan and engineering comments tie the dropout to electrolyte loss and high cell impedance. The team itself calls this one of several possible factors, so confidence is medium.
notes: Multi-incident master ticket; individual incident tickets (VXEP-1435, 1413, 1398, 1293, 1417, 1499) and RMA-797 were not read since the cause is consolidated here and in BAT-367. Teardown deck titles the cells AE7844152XT 4400mAh while the Root Cause field says 3300mAh cells. VXEP-1622 tracks further PMA263 HLB dropouts (VXE 865, 852, 639). Tail list taken from the battery status table.

event: VXE-557 (USASOC) could not take off because the GCS 6.5 status panel showed a fuel cell firmware update error; logs also held a genuine low temperature fuel cell fault.
component: GCS 6.5 fuel cell firmware update detection
failure_mode: false firmware update message because the detection compares the wrong build name
contributing: genuine fuel cell fault 25632, temperature inside fuel cell below operational threshold
fuel cell later returned under RMA for Advisory Notice 25-005

evidence.quote: There is an issue detecting fuel cell firmware updates.
We will need to investigate why the firmware update detection uses the wrong ‘Build Name’.
Both AARs contain fuel cell logs with the following error: 25632 Temperature inside Fuel Cell Below Operational Threshold.
the original fuel cell from the report seemed to have other issues.
GCSS-444: Fuel Cell Erroneous Update Detected

team_view_in_comments: We will need to investigate why the firmware update detection uses the wrong ‘Build Name’.

would_settle_it.what: which message blocked takeoff: the update message or the low temperature fault
software fix and confirmation of the build name comparison bug (ticket has no content yet)

reasoning: The GCS lead found that the update detection uses the wrong build name, which explains the erroneous update message, and opened bug GCSS-444 against 6.5.0. Separately the logs show a real cold fuel cell fault that could also have prevented takeoff. The software defect is identified but not confirmed fixed, and it is not clear which of the two messages actually stopped the launch.
notes: Two issues on one ticket. RMA-758 covers eight USASOC fuel cells (D4500604 and others) returned for Advisory Notice 25-005; the ticket does not say which serial was on VXE-557. Closed Won't Do.

event: New E140 gimbal assemblies with the new regulator payload harness gave no or poor video on VXE30 and VXE35 aircraft and iron birds because of heavy ethernet packet loss.
component: E140ZG2 interface board / payload harness ethernet link (2125741-01)
failure_mode: about half of ethernet packets lost between aircraft and gimbal; suspected capacitor coupled (no magnetics) back-to-back PHY link and unshielded wiring
contributing: harnesses only acceptance tested on a ground support cable, not on an aircraft
unshielded harness wire
possible EMI and grounding on Block 30 aircraft

evidence.quote: We did some pings and we're losing probably half the packets when connected to an aircraft or an IB.
Here is the problematic capacitor isolation that is a likley cause/contributor to this issue and many others.
Every cable was tested in production on a G2 with the new Alden ground support cable - they all worked fine (and still do).
Will continue to try to work this PHY issue after getting the next revision out to the PCB house.
This rev will implement an ethernet switch rather than the back-to-back PHYs.

team_view_in_comments: Here is the problematic capacitor isolation that is a likley cause/contributor to this issue and many others.

would_settle_it.file: Investigation Summary test plan and data New E140 Assemblies video not working DCDC getting hot during operation.xlsx
would_settle_it.what: cause summary tab and magnetics or switch test results
whether the V2 interface board with an ethernet switch cured the packet loss in production

reasoning: Pings showed about 50% packet loss only when the new harness was on an aircraft or iron bird, across several gimbals, while the same cables passed on a ground support cable. Engineers suspected the capacitor isolated ethernet without magnetics, and the Rev B interface board replaced the back-to-back PHYs with an ethernet switch and was reported to work well. This narrows the cause to the interface board ethernet design, but no single test in the files isolates PHY coupling from shielding or EMI.
notes: Comment from 2025-07-24 is a pasted Teams chat with repeated lines. VA-2855 reports 'works well' without test details. Not read: VXEP-1486, 1497, 1509, 1318, PLD-55, VA-2865, VA-2873, VA-2874 (design or related incident tickets).

event: During a TIQUILA VXE-626 mission about 8 km out, the GCS became jumpy, repeatedly re-synced mission elements, loaded an old mission and lost positive control, so the crew flew it back in U-Drive and recovered it undamaged.
component: GCS mission element sync and zone overlays
failure_mode: repeated sim and sync every 4 to 5 seconds, old mission repopulated, mission elements deleted from display when zone overlays added
contributing: zone overlays uploaded before the event
possible radio link degradation at about 8 km
GCS software restarted mid flight

evidence.quote: the GCS became JUMPY in area 12 (approx 8km from the GCS), and started populating mission elements (ORBIT HERE NOW) and repeatedly conducting SIM AND SYNC, roughly every 4-5 seconds.
We conducted the download but despite saving the mission, it populated a previous mission outside of our AO (Area of Operations).
We noticed that when Zone Overlays were added, it caused the GCS to behave abnormally, again to be JUMPY and it deleted some of the Mission Elements from the GCS screen.
However despite not displaying ORBIT 3 on the GCS, the UA continued to Orbit in the location commanded and at the altitude.
None of the GCS logs or settings are included so there’s almost nothing to investigate.

would_settle_it.file: GCS AAR with GCS logs and settings
would_settle_it.what: mission sync messages and errors at the time of the jumpy behavior
the overlays uploaded before the event, to reproduce the abnormal behavior
link quality and mission upload traffic in the XCOMM and VTOL logs

reasoning: The aircraft kept flying the commanded orbit while the GCS display lost elements, and the abnormal behavior returned when zone overlays were added, which points at the GCS mission handling rather than the aircraft. No GCS logs or overlay files were ever provided, so the specific module and trigger cannot be shown, and a link problem at range is not ruled out.
notes: Only XCOMM and VTOL data were attached (not converted); closed by backlogging without investigation.

event: On the ground, VXE-881 repeatedly lost connection with its MCM and XCOMM (apparent resets) during payload power up while testing a new Epsilon payload cable.
failure_mode: MCM reboots (PMC reset), also triggered by hot plugging the gimbal
contributing: hot plugging the gimbal reboots the MCM
EMI or grounding with 40 to 60% packet loss on Block 30 aircraft
faulty DC/DC board in payload harness
MCM clock not set, making log timing unclear

evidence.quote: Instance 3: approximately ten seconds after the epsilon finished its BIT after a power cycle, lost connection to everything again, no chirp
Note that the syslog shows that 881’s MCM has booted 55 times on May 5
PMC Reset error - I believe is tied to MCM partitioning being configured incorrectly.
After Alan and I reconfigured the MCM, we haven’t seen the PMC Reset after that in the SYSLog
hot plugging the gimbal will cause the MCM to reboot.
We experienced 60-40% packet loss over 15 minutes.

team_view_in_comments: PMC Reset error - I believe is tied to MCM partitioning being configured incorrectly.

would_settle_it.what: the PMC reset error lines in syslog and their timing against the reported instances
boot events and PMC reset errors at the reported times
production write up of the MCM partitioning misconfiguration (also NCC-168, NCC-161, not in export)
crash dump or timestamp reset proving whether XCOMM actually reset

reasoning: Syslog shows the MCM booting many times, and the engineer saw PMC reset errors that stopped after the MCM partitioning was reconfigured, which points to a misconfigured MCM. Hot plugging the gimbal and EMI on the new cable were also shown to disturb the MCM or link, and none of the four instances was tied to a specific log event because the clock was wrong. The cause is narrowed to the MCM configuration with other payload related candidates remaining; it was closed as not verifiable.
notes: Four instances on one ticket, all during payload power up with no user inputs. It was never confirmed whether XCOMM reset or only the network dropped. The closing comment suggests new gimbal mounts as corrective action, which does not match the findings. NCC-174, NCC-168, NCC-161 are not in the export.
